| Large 40 m | 3 drones | 79.1% | — | not reached | 79.0% | 0.1% / 1.0% | 0.00 |
| Large 40 m | 3 drones, no radio (each flies alone) | 32.8% | −46.3 pts (95% CI −49.2 pts to −43.1 pts) | not reached | 0.0% | 16.6% / 32.8% | 0.20 |
| Large 40 m | 3 drones, shared maps, no frontier split | 75.9% | −3.3 pts (95% CI −4.6 pts to −1.8 pts) | not reached | 75.7% | 0.1% / 1.1% | 0.00 |
| Large 40 m | 3 drones, perfect radio | 79.1% | −0.0 pts (95% CI −0.0 pts to +0.0 pts) | not reached | 79.1% | 0.0% / 0.1% | 0.00 |
| Large 40 m | 2 explorers + 1 relay | 58.4% | −20.7 pts (95% CI −21.9 pts to −19.2 pts) | not reached | 58.4% | 0.0% / 0.3% | 0.00 |
| Large 40 m | 3 drones, weak radio (-10 dBm) | 79.1% | +0.0 pts (95% CI −0.3 pts to +0.4 pts) | not reached | 76.7% | 1.1% / 7.5% | 0.00 |
| Large 40 m | 2 explorers + 1 relay, weak radio (-10 dBm) | 56.5% | −22.6 pts (95% CI −24.1 pts to −21.1 pts) | not reached | 55.9% | 0.2% / 2.1% | 0.00 |

- **Sharing maps is most of the gain.** Without the radio each drone explores alone and covers what the others already did: −46.3 pts (95% CI −49.2 pts to −43.1 pts) against the full team on large buildings, and overlap near 2.7.
- **Splitting frontiers adds a few points and keeps drones apart.** Without claims the drones share maps but chase the same frontiers: −3.3 pts (95% CI −4.6 pts to −1.8 pts), and they spend many more steps within 0.35 m of each other.
- **The radio limits what the base knows, not how much gets searched.** A perfect radio changes coverage by −0.0 pts (95% CI −0.0 pts to +0.0 pts). With the 0 dBm radio the base trails the truth by 0.1% / 1.0% (mean / worst); with the −10 dBm radio by 1.1% / 7.5%.
- **Energy follows drone count, and no pack runs low.** The battery column integrates the power model from the speed study (`DEFAULT_BATTERY`, the airframe's 35.7 Wh pack) over each drone's flight. A 240 s search never uses more than 27.5% of any drone's usable pack, so endurance does not bind at this budget; time does. Searched points per team Wh fall slowly with team size on large buildings (3.6 for one drone, 3.0 for four), because extra drones spend some of their flight on ground a teammate already covered. Without the radio, each searched point costs more than twice the energy.
- **A dedicated relay is not worth a drone here.** On the weak radio it changes the worst awareness gap by −5.4 pts (95% CI −7.3 pts to −3.8 pts) (0.2% / 2.1% against 1.1% / 7.5%) and coverage by −22.6 pts (95% CI −24.1 pts to −21.1 pts). Three explorers already chain the link back to the base most of the time. A relay should pay where the building is deeper than the team can chain, or where an operator needs a live picture more than a fast one.

The live page (`team.html`) runs this code in the browser: the truth beside what the base sees, with the radio links drawn.

## Search by sight

Every mission above detects with an *analytic* camera: a recall curve over distance, light and blur, and a dice roll, with no pixels (`src/perception/detector.ts`). This section replaces it with a camera and a learned detector and flies the same missions again.

### Method

**Camera** (`src/vision/scene.ts`). A software rasterizer draws the drone's view at 160×120 from the same world the missions fly: walls with door and window cut-outs, floors, furniture, terrain, trees, people and objects. Shading has the sun, room lights and the drone's flashlight cone; a sensor model sets exposure from the scene, adds read noise that grows with gain, and quantizes to 8 bits, so night frames are dark and grainy. The renderer also writes a depth image and an instance image. The instance image is used only for labels and for scoring; the drone never reads it. It runs in Node and in the browser at about 4 ms a frame.

**People** are the CC0 KayKit mannequin ([CREDITS.md](../CREDITS.md)) baked into ten poses (standing, sitting, lying, hiding and six walking frames) by `scripts/vision/bake-humanoid.mjs`. The pose, shirt colour and turn match the 3D view. Decoys look different from what they imitate: the mannequin is plain grey plastic, and the real backpack and toolbox have a flap, straps or a handle that their look-alikes lack. The same details are in the 3D view.

**Detector** (`src/vision/detector.ts`). A CenterNet-style convolutional network with about 180k parameters reads the 160×120 frame and outputs, on a 20×15 grid, a heatmap for each of nine classes (person and eight objects) and a box size and offset. Decoys are trained as background. It is trained in TF.js with focal loss on 32,000 frames (80 per world), rendered from worlds 66001–66400 with random surface colours, shirt colours and light levels on three worlds in four. The checkpoint is the epoch with the lowest loss on practice frames from worlds 66501–66560. Confidences are calibrated on the same practice frames with a two-parameter logistic fit.

**From box to contact** (`src/vision/source.ts`). Each detection above a calibrated confidence of 0.3 becomes a contact. Its position is the ray through the box centre at the range of the nearest surface the depth image sees inside the box, plus 15 cm to the body centre and 3% noise. The camera is assumed to be RGB-D. Everything after that is unchanged: the same tracker, the same three-bearing confirmation at the same threshold, and the same re-view flights. Which space counts as looked at is still estimated geometrically, as before.

### Detector on fresh frames

On 2,400 frames (1520 day, 880 night) from fresh worlds 67001–67060 the detector scores a mean AP of 0.61 at IoU 0.5, 0.77 for people. Calibration brings the expected calibration error from 0.088 to 0.008. It fires on empty background 0.003 times a frame and called a mannequin a person 0 of 387 times it saw one; it called the decoy pack a backpack 1 of 45 times. It takes 1.9 ms a frame on the CPU with TF.js's native backend.

| Class | AP at IoU 0.5 | Labelled boxes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Person | 0.77 | 658 |
| Backpack | 0.50 | 60 |
| Phone | 0.00 | 16 |
| Toolbox | 0.85 | 60 |
| Medkit | 0.62 | 41 |
| Bottle | 0.99 | 18 |
| Radio | 0.47 | 14 |
| Helmet | 0.71 | 46 |
| Blanket | 0.62 | 60 |

Recall at a calibrated confidence of 0.5, by distance (labelled boxes in brackets):

| Distance | Person, day | Person, night | Objects, day | Objects, night |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–2 m | 80% (101) | 88% (40) | 64% (53) | 50% (18) |
| 2–4 m | 83% (166) | 87% (55) | 55% (122) | 74% (46) |
| 4–6 m | 62% (111) | 67% (30) | 53% (36) | 53% (17) |
| 6–8 m | 64% (28) | 56% (18) | 43% (7) | 0% (3) |
| 8–10 m | 78% (9) | 70% (10) | 20% (5) | 0% (1) |
| 10–14 m | 59% (17) | 50% (10) | 0% (3) | — |

### Missions with the camera

Each scenario is flown on 30 fresh worlds (67201–67230) with both indoor explorers, once with the analytic detector and once with the camera, 180 camera flights in all. Contact gating was set on practice worlds 66601–66616 and not changed after.

Since missions stopped reading ground truth, a building is clear only when no contact is still open there. A one-frame false detection the camera placed in a building's wall had no free point around it to be looked at again from, so it stayed open and the building could never be declared clear: on the first reported block (67101–67130), re-flown after that change, the camera met the expected outcome on only 61.7% of compound sweeps. The last look before leaving a building now re-views such a contact from the nearest free point, and rejects it when nothing in the drone's own map can see it. Found on the practice worlds only, it is reported on this fresh block. On the same 180 paired flights, the code before the fix scores 65.0% on camera compound sweeps and 82.8% on all camera flights, with no false clear either way.

| Scenario | Detector | Expected outcome (95% CI) | Mean time to first find | Mean flight | False alarms | False clears |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cabin search, day** | Analytic detector | 100.0% (94–100%) | 140 s | 187 s | 0 | 0 |
|  | Camera + learned detector | 100.0% (94–100%) | 135 s | 179 s | 0 | 0 |
| **Two-building safety sweep** | Analytic detector | 96.7% (89–99%) | — | 1011 s | 0 | 0 |
|  | Camera + learned detector | 88.3% (78–94%) | — | 935 s | 0 | 0 |
| **Backpack search, night** | Analytic detector | 100.0% (94–100%) | 162 s | 206 s | 0 | 0 |
|  | Camera + learned detector | 98.3% (91–100%) | 196 s | 247 s | 1 | 0 |

**What the numbers say.** Over all 180 paired flights the camera meets the expected outcome in 95.6% against 98.9% for the analytic detector. 6 paired flights succeed only with the analytic detector and 0 only with the camera, so the camera never rescues a flight the analytic model loses.

The two are within noise of each other in every scenario; the night backpack is 98.3% against 100.0%. Under the flashlight alone the detector often scores the backpack around 0.4 to 0.6, below the 0.8 mean the three-bearing confirmation asks for, so the drone spends its re-views on it. The confirmation threshold was left where the analytic missions set it. An earlier run of this bench showed a much larger night gap; most of it was targets the placer had put inside tables and shelves, hidden from the camera but not from the analytic detector, which has no furniture occlusion. Targets are now never placed inside furniture.

Camera flights confirmed a decoy or declared a building clear with a target inside only rarely (1 false alarm, 0 false clears in 180 flights). A camera flight renders and reads about 2,267 frames and takes 35 s of wall time on one CPU core, against 4 s with the analytic detector.

## Failure atlas

The mission bench flies a few fixed scenarios, so it can only find the failures someone thought to stage. The failure atlas asks instead how often the shipped autopilot (`policyQuad`: the policy indoors with the sensor-only planner as backup, on the quadrotor, with the operator approving every entry) fails over a declared distribution of 16 mission dimensions: the mission kind, the number of buildings, the person's pose, objects and decoys, interior lights, time of day, wind and gusts, and a sensor or airframe fault on 40% of flights with its onset and severity. The full method, the conditional rates and every failing flight are in [ATLAS.md](ATLAS.md) and on the [atlas page](https://alexnieves-cs.github.io/frontier-fly/atlas.html), where each one replays in the browser.

**Method.** A cross-entropy search (6,800 flights) learns a proposal distribution that makes each failure common, scored by how close a flight came to it. Fresh flights drawn from a mixture of that proposal and the nominal distribution then give an importance-sampled rate, and plain Monte Carlo on its own seeds checks it. No seed block used here is used by any other study, and nothing was tuned on them. The rates below are a re-run of the two importance-sampled estimates and the Monte Carlo check on fresh seeds (255001–267000) with the current code: unresolved contacts ([below](#unresolved-contacts)), the one airframe and the policy retrained under the crash rule. The proposal is still the one the search learned at v1.0.0.

| Event | Importance sampling (95% CI) | Plain Monte Carlo (95% CI) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| False clear | 0.25% (0.16% to 0.35%), 2,000 flights | 0.20% (0.11% to 0.35%), 12 of 6,000 |
| Collision | 1.15% (0.77% to 1.72%) | 1.22% (0.97% to 1.53%) |

**Where the false clears are.** All of them are on sweeps of an occupied site, where the drone's job is to confirm clear and a person is inside: 0.8% (0.5% to 1.4%) of those flights. On every mission with someone or something to find the rate is 0.3%. Find-a-person and find-an-object missions had none. The person's pose decides it: across all flights a walking person is falsely cleared on 0.1% and a hiding one on 0.9%, against 0.0% for a person standing, sitting or lying (12 of 12 false clears had a moving or hiding person). In the cases traced the detector does see the person, with confidences around 0.7 to 0.9 on single views, but the confirmation rule averages repeated views and the average never reaches the confirm bar, so the contact is rejected and the building is called clear. The earlier mission bench reported 1 false clear in 360 flights because its occupied sweep only ever placed a person lying still.

**Collisions** have no single driver. The worst slices, a sagging battery and a silent lidar, are about twice the mean, and most contacts happen while the drone leaves or explores a building.

### Unresolved contacts

The first atlas run measured the code at v1.0.0, where 3.55% of flights (importance-sampled) were false clears. Its false clears came from the confirmation rule: a person track that ran out of re-views short of the bar was rejected, and nothing then stood in the way of a clear. Two changes followed (`src/mission/autonomy/planner/confirm.ts`, `phases/search.ts`):

- **Unresolved, not rejected.** A track that runs out of re-views closes as *rejected* only when its views score no better than a lookalike does. Otherwise it is *unresolved*: it stays live (a later view can still confirm it), it blocks a clear of the building it is in, and the mission report lists it for a person to check. The floor is 0.70 mean confidence, set on a dev block (240001-240240) where decoy tracks closed at 0.48 to 0.68 and the real people the drone failed to confirm at 0.62 to 0.80. It belongs to this simulated detector, as the confirm threshold does; a different detector needs its own.
- **Tracks that follow a walker.** A person track's estimate leans on its newest contacts, its association gate grows at walking speed while it is unseen (up to 4 m), and two tracks of one walker that were never seen in the same frame are merged. People are re-viewed from 3.2 m first instead of 2.2 m: motion blur in the detector model falls with distance, so a walker scores higher a little farther away.

Both versions flew the same 2,000 fresh flights (seeds 250001-252000, plain Monte Carlo from the atlas's nominal distribution, flown once after tuning; the new code at `f609dc8`, the control at `d881b47`).

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| False clear, per flight | 4.05% (3.27% to 5.01%), 81 flights | 0.30% (0.14% to 0.65%), 6 flights |
| False clear, sweeps of an occupied site | 15.3% | 1.1% |
| Mission ends as expected | 44.4% | 45.1% |
| Walking person found (find and sweep missions) | 27 of 251 | 63 of 251 |
| Hiding person found | 91 of 230 | 79 of 230 |
| Empty sweep cleared | 179 of 380 | 176 of 380 |
| Collision, per flight | 2.55% | 2.35% |

What it costs: a sweep with an unresolved person ends *incomplete* rather than *found*, so most of the former false clears became incomplete sweeps, not finds. Hiding people are found less often than before, and a few empty sweeps no longer clear. Every remaining false clear has a hiding person whose views averaged 0.66 to 0.69, inside the band decoys also reach: this detector cannot tell them from a mannequin, and only a better detector or more views would.

## Doors, glass and smoke

Until now every interior door stood open and door leaves were only drawn. Three hazards now change what the drone can fly through and what its sensors return, each with its own seed block, pass condition and bench row (`src/gen/hazards.ts`, applied after generation and seeded by the building):

- **Doors.** A share of interior doorways is shut: the leaf becomes a wall cell with a door surface, and a shut door is never opened. A shut door that leaves less than half the building reachable is opened again. Most of the others get a thin leaf standing ajar at 30–75°, a collidable obstacle in the doorway. Coverage counts only what is reachable with the doors as they are.
- **Glass and mirrors.** The inner walls of some rooms turn to glass, where a lidar beam drops out 35% of the time and reads as max range, and a few interior wall faces become mirrors that return the reflected path, so the wall reads further away than it is.
- **Smoke.** Some rooms fill with smoke of visibility 1.5–4 m. A horizontal lidar beam crossing smoke can come back early, and the camera detector's recall falls with the smoke's transmittance along the line of sight.

The explorers know hazards exist but not where. With hazard awareness on, a mission logs every shut door it sees whose far side it has not searched and will not call a building clear while one is left; it tells the operator a ground team is needed. It skips smoke-filled voxels when it scores a look, and it never rejects a contact seen in smoke: the contact is left unresolved, which blocks the clear. The unaware control flies the same code with all three switched off.

**Coverage.** The hard-building coverage study flies each hazard on fresh stage-3 buildings 86001–86030 (day), paired with the same buildings without hazards. The pass condition, fixed before the run: the sensor-only planner and the guarded policy each keep at least 90% of their own no-hazard coverage and crash on at most 2 of 30 flights, in every hazard (crash = contact at 0.5 m/s or more). Cells give mean coverage, then crashes of 30 in brackets, then the ratio to the pilot's own control.

- **No false clear in 360 flights, but the control had 1.**  Aware flights stopped short of a clear because of a shut door they could not search behind in 2 flights. Every room of a mission shell also has its own outside opening, so a shut interior door slows the search but cannot hide anyone from a drone that goes round; a person truly sealed behind a door needs a building the generator does not make yet.
- **Smoke is the gap.** The hiker in a smoky cabin is found on 14 of 30 flights by every explorer, aware or not, and occupied sweeps in smoke end incomplete on 16–19 of 30: the camera loses the person and the lidar's early returns shrink the free space the drone will fly into. Awareness keeps those flights honest (incomplete, not clear) but does not find the person; that needs a sensor that sees through smoke, such as thermal, which the drone does not carry.
- **The crash bar was set below the guarded policy's own control.** It crashes on 1 of 30 of these buildings with no hazards at all, so its hazard misses on crashes say more about the bar than about the hazards; its coverage stays within 81.5% of the control. The bar is kept as it was set.
- **Thin ajar leaves catch the oracle teacher.** It reads the true map and crashes on 10 of 30 door buildings against 0 without hazards; the ajar leaves are the only new obstacle there. The sensor-only planner, which sees them with its lidar, does not crash.

## Negative results and limitations

- **The drone falsely clears moving and hiding people.** About one in eight sweeps of an occupied site ends with the building declared clear, almost always with a walking or hiding person the detector did see. The fix is in the confirmation rule (a moving contact should be re-acquired, not averaged), not in the detector, and it is not attempted here.
- **Imitation alone is bounded by its teacher.** The DAgger policy imitates an oracle that sees the floor plan, yet on fresh hard buildings it did not beat a planner that sees only lidar. Only PPO on its own flights took it past both, and it still collides where the planner does not.
- **The policy alone still crashes more than under its guard.** Retraining under the crash rule cut its crashes on the 30 fresh hard buildings from 19 to 7 of 30 by day, but it now bumps walls slowly far more often than before, and the lidar guard still removes most of the remaining crashes. The guard stays on in missions and on the homepage.
- **Only the planner climbs.** The teacher and the policy still chase ground-floor frontiers on multi-floor buildings. The planner's floor share is a fixed rule, not a plan over the whole building.
- **The policy barely flies the quadrotor.** It is now trained with half of its flights on randomized quadrotor dynamics, which lifts its quad coverage from 4% to about 20%, but most of its quad flights still end in a crash, where the quad-aware planner has none. A velocity command that assumes the airframe stops at once is the wrong interface for a drone that brakes by tilting; a policy that outputs attitude, or one trained with the braking filter in the loop, is not attempted.
- **The planner is not the best explorer by every measure.** It ties a textbook boustrophedon sweep on the bench score. By the footprint, the way exploration papers count coverage, a 2016 next-best-view planner (NBVP) sees more of the building and sees it sooner ([Against published exploration methods](#against-published-exploration-methods)). The bench score rewards flying through voxels, which the planner and the policy were built for. A search that only needs the camera within 3 m would be better served by a next-best-view goal.
- **The braking model is fitted, not derived.** Its two constants come from simulated stopping tests on the randomized airframes. A heavier airframe, a stronger wind or a slower controller needs them measured again.
- **Night confirmation is near the detector's ceiling.** Under the flashlight alone the per-frame confidence barely clears the 0.8 threshold, so confirmation needs several clean bearings. A target boxed in by furniture can leave too few.
- **Entry is conservative by design.** When no opening is safe enough, the drone does not enter and the sweep stays incomplete. That costs success rate and never a false clear.
- **The lost-person prior is not what makes the outdoor search fast.** Sweep-width lanes, a distance ring and a flat prior all do about as well by day. The strategy weights and ring sizes are hand-set, not fitted to incident data, and the simulated walker that places the person was written alongside the prior, so even this agreement is optimistic.
- **The search belief is miscalibrated.** It credits a building interior only once the drone leaves it, so by day it trails the outcomes early (78% predicted by 90 s against 87% found). It also trusts its prior: with the person placed uniformly it predicts 95% success and 78% of searches succeed.
- **Teams fly a simple world.** Drones in a team cannot collide physically (they keep apart with a velocity filter, and the bench counts close passes: 2164 steps within 0.35 m over every team episode, mostly around the shared entry). They share a radio channel with no contention, all fly the kinematic airframe by day. The bench reports battery energy. A drone turns back along its own track once its energy used plus 1.5 times its estimated way home would empty the pack (`packWh` in `src/team/run.ts`), but none comes close in 240 s, so the bench never exercises it; a unit test does, with a 1.2 Wh pack.
- **The quadrotor can't use a faster cruise.** The planner steers with pure pursuit and a velocity command, which suits a drone that changes velocity almost instantly. A simple corner-speed tracker didn't help, and the evidence points to the airframe's acceleration (about 3 m/s² at the controller's tilt limit) rather than the planner. A full minimum-time trajectory planner, or a stiffer airframe, is untested.
- **The camera is a renderer, not a photograph.** People are one low-poly mannequin in ten poses with a coloured shirt, objects are boxes with a few details, and the detector trains and tests on the same renderer. Its scores say nothing about real images. Range comes from a perfect depth image plus 3% noise, and which space counts as looked at is still estimated geometrically, not from the detector.
- **Phones are not found.** The detector's AP for phones is near zero; at 160×120 a phone is a few pixels. No mission asks for one.
- **Some sensor models are simple.** The opening sensor and the aperture tracker are error models of a depth camera and a visual tracker, not image processing, and GNSS is RTK-grade with no multipath near walls. A rougher sensor would cost entries before it cost false clears: confirm-clear rests on the drone's own maps, not on these.
- **Confirm-clear is only as good as the look estimate.** A building is declared clear when at least 95% of the free voxels the drone mapped and can reach on each floor were looked at by its camera estimate, so up to 5% of a floor can go unlooked. Space the lidar never mapped (behind furniture taller than the ring, or under a table) is not counted, and the detector can still miss a person in looked-at space. The occupied sweep measures the result, on one target pose per world.
- **The estimate is less safe on the quadrotor.** In the closed-loop table above, the quadrotor flying on the estimate touches something in more flights than any other arm and than the same explorer on the true pose, mostly in the compound sweeps; the cause has not been traced, and the kinematic arms on the estimate are not affected.
- **The coverage study's policy and planner never fly on the estimate.** Only the mission bench does; the coverage numbers above are on the true pose.
- **The localization sensors are idealized in places.** Each lidar sweep is instantaneous (no motion distortion), the flow sensor's errors are white plus a per-flight scale error, walls are perfectly flat and axis-aligned (which the Manhattan heading fix relies on), and nothing in the building moves. The drone's estimator has no loop closure in flight: drift that enters the map stays in it. The loop closer was tried behind it offline, on 24 of the drone's own flights in the estimator's tuning buildings (`scripts/study/loc-loop.ts`), and made the pose worse: 15 cm from the drone's own map against 5 cm for the filter alone, with no setting tried closing the gap. These buildings are a few rooms across and the filter's single map already stays consistent in them, and a 90-beam ring gives the graph's keyframe matches less to hold on to than the Intel robot's 180 beams at 1°. So missions do not use it.
- **The footprint is an idealized sensor.** It is a 360° ring of perfect rays in the lidar plane: no field-of-view limit, no lighting, no motion blur, and nothing above or below the drone's altitude. A forward camera with a narrow field of view would score lower and would reward pilots that turn to look. It measures what came into view, not whether a target there would have been recognized.
- **One simulator, one real log.** Everything here is measured in this repository's simulator; nothing has flown on hardware. The one real data the code has seen is the Intel Research Lab laser log, which only the pose estimator replays (above), and on it the filter alone drifts metres over the 45-minute run while the loop closer matches published graph SLAM.

## Reproduce

```bash
npm ci
npm run study:coverage   # docs/study.json: every pilot, 30 fresh buildings per condition, flown and footprint coverage
npm run study:missions   # docs/mission-bench.json: each indoor explorer, airframe and pose source, 30 fresh worlds per scenario
npm run study:team       # docs/team-bench.json and docs/report/team-curves.svg: 1 to 4 drones and the team ablations
npm run study:sar        # docs/sar-bench.json and docs/report/sar-belief.svg: six outdoor search methods
npm run train:ppo -- --init public/checkpoints/pretrained.bin --out ppo.bin   # PPO fine-tune (see scripts/train-ppo.ts for the shipped recipe)
vite-node scripts/study/rl-finetune.ts -- dagger=old.bin ppo=ppo.bin   # docs/rl-finetune.json
npm run study:speed      # docs/speed-study.json: coverage and energy at speed caps of 2 to 5 m/s
npm run study:plans      # docs/plans-bench.json: real apartments against same-size generated buildings
npm run bench:board      # bench/results/*.json: every FrontierBench baseline on the test split
npm run bench:team -- --board   # bench/results/team/*.json: the baseline drone teams
npm install --no-save @tensorflow/tfjs-node@4.22.0   # native TF.js for the camera scripts
npm run study:vision     # docs/vision-bench.json: missions with the camera and the learned detector
# Camera detector: scripts/vision/make-dataset.ts, train-detector.ts and eval-detector.ts (see their headers)
npm run study:loc        # docs/localization.json: pose estimator arms over 120 fresh flights
npm run study:intel      # docs/intel-lab.json: the same estimator on the real Intel Research Lab log (data/intel-lab/)
vite-node scripts/study/gallery.ts          # docs/report/*.svg
# Ablations: one train:indoor run per arm, then scripts/study/ablations.ts (see its header)
npm run docs             # re-render this page, BENCHMARKS.md and the README
```
